overview: The two structural categories of fatty acid, distinguished by carbon-carbon bonding and with real consequences for physical properties and health.
genZNote: Saturated: straight and stackable. Unsaturated: kinked and can't sit still.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: Fatty acids with no carbon-carbon double bonds — every carbon is "saturated" with hydrogen.
aspects.valueB: Fatty acids containing one (monounsaturated) or more (polyunsaturated) carbon-carbon double bonds.

aspects.label: Structure
aspects.valueA: Straight hydrocarbon chain, allowing tight packing.
aspects.valueB: Kinked chain at each double bond (typically cis configuration), preventing tight packing.

aspects.label: Physical State at Room Temperature
aspects.valueB: Typically liquid (e.g. olive oil, fish oil).

aspects.label: Common Dietary Sources
aspects.valueA: Animal fats, butter, coconut oil, palm oil.
aspects.valueB: Plant oils (olive, canola), nuts, seeds, fatty fish (omega-3s).

aspects.label: Health Association
aspects.valueA: Higher intake is generally associated with raised LDL cholesterol when consumed in excess.
aspects.valueB: Generally associated with favorable lipid profiles, especially polyunsaturated omega-3 and omega-6 fats.

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueA: No double bonds, straight chain, solid at room temperature.
aspects.valueB: One or more double bonds, kinked chain, liquid at room temperature.
